AITech LabHow the talk runs
How the talk runs

A theory tour of agents

Why now

Intelligence as a commodity, the numbers already in production, the trajectory and the economics.

What an agent is

Not a chatbot — a loop: gather context, take action, verify, repeat. Agent = model + harness.

The harness

Memory, skills, tools (MCP), orchestration, context. Designing an agent is software engineering.

From a loop to loops

Don’t prompt agents to write code — build loops that run themselves. Kinds of loops, self-driving products.

Trust: evals

How you know it works: re-running production, LLM-as-judge, the SRE mindset.

Two ways to build

Feature work (brainstorm → grill → understand) and autonomous loops (research → MVP → eval → relaunch).

AITech LabThe shift underneath everything
The shift underneath everything

Intelligence is now a commodity

Until now

Buying intelligence meant hiring someone.

Today

You buy it like a raw material.

Raw intelligence only talks. An agent is what puts it to work, acting on the world to deliver value with it. That is what this talk is about.

AITech LabTrajectory
Trajectory

Agents run longer and longer on their own

Length of tasks completed autonomously · 50% success
Source: METR, time-horizon benchmark

In 2023, an agent could hold a task for a few minutes. Today it holds hours of autonomous work.

A clean exponential: the autonomy window doubles roughly every seven months, about 3× faster than Moore's Law, and it has not bent yet. [1][2]

AITech LabThe anatomy
The anatomy · stepped

Agent = LLM + harness

LLM

The reasoning engine. Brilliant, but alone it can only talk. You buy that part; everything else is the harness.

01 Instructions

CLAUDE.md, standing instructions read at every session.

02 Tools

How it touches the world: CLI, APIs, MCP connectors.

03 Memory

What it keeps between sessions, plain files first.

04 Skills

Recipes it knows how to follow, plain markdown.

05 Sandbox

Where its code runs, and how far it can reach.

06 Orchestration

Subagents it briefs, runs and coordinates.

The harness is what turns a model that talks into a system that acts.[1] The parts that matter: context, memory & skills, orchestration.

AITech LabThe harness · Orchestration
The harness · Orchestration

Sub-agents vs parallel — agents that multiply

Sub-agent

A child with its own context window. The main agent hands off a bounded task and gets back only a summary — the verbose work never pollutes the main loop. It’s delegation + context isolation.

Parallel

Many agents at once — concurrency: throughput on independent work. Orthogonal to sub-agents — run them one after another, or fan them out.

→

Rule of thumb: independent work → parallel; dependent work (B needs A) → sequence; research & audits → background. A vague hand-off fails — give the sub-agent full context at dispatch.

Source: ClaudeFast — sub-agent best practices
AITech LabLoops · why now
Loops · why now

Why now — real capability gains

The harness is assembled — but you don’t drive it by hand. You build loops. And they work now, on real capability gains, not hype:

  • Models are better at long tasks — METR: Opus 4.6 completes 50% of 12-hour tasks, ~6× Opus 4. The autonomy window is what loops cash in.
  • Huge tasks already shipped — a Stripe codebase migration in a day (vs ~2 months by hand); Lovable one-shots apps.
  • Loops are built in — Claude Code /loop, automations, the Ralph plugin. You no longer hand-roll the loop.
  • Subagents separate the loop from the work — the loop driver stays small while subagents do the heavy lifting: saves tokens, prevents context degradation.
  • Harnesses are maturing — compaction, skills + MCP, cloud execution. The infrastructure caught up to the idea.
Source: PostHog — "Why we're bullish on loops", Ian Vanagas
AITech LabLoops · the thesis
Loops · the thesis

Don't prompt agents to write code — build loops

The thesis: Don't prompt agents to write code one task at a time. Build LOOPS that prompt themselves — so agents do long-running tasks, and so you can run many of them in parallel.

Two builders converging on the same idea, independently:

Peter Steinberger · OpenClaw

Loops as the way to keep an agent productive over long horizons.

Boris Cherny · Claude Code

Loops built into the harness itself.

The shift: from "write this for me" (one prompt, one task) to "keep working toward this" (a loop that re-prompts itself until the goal is met). Anthropic’s Claude Code team defines it exactly so: “loops = agents repeating cycles of work until a stop condition is met.”

Source: Anthropic — “Getting started with loops” (Claude Code team) · PostHog — Ian Vanagas.
AITech LabLoops · in the wild
Loops · in the wild · stepped

Loops in the wild — what people run

Whatever the kind, a loop needs a goal and a way to verify — “a loop without a goal is a slop cannon.”

PR babysitter

Watches a pull request and shepherds it to green.

/loop "watch PR #2034 — fix failures until CI is green"

Bug fixer

Reproduces, isolates, fixes, verifies — on its own.

/goal "reproduce & fix issue #881, add a regression test"

Flaky-test hunter

Finds and stabilises non-deterministic tests.

/loop "find a flaky test, stabilise it — one per run"

Perf autoresearcher

Karpathy’s fixed a 3-year-old bug, +11% perf.

/goal "profile the hot path, propose & benchmark a fix"
Types: Anthropic — “Getting started with loops”. “Slop cannon”: PostHog — Ian Vanagas.
AITech LabLoops · the SOTA loop
Loops · the SOTA loop · stepped

Planner · Generator · Evaluator — the loop Anthropic runs

PM Planner own context window

One-line spec → a deliberately high-level series of sprints. Vague on purpose — granular plans make errors cascade over a multi-hour run.

/goal "Kanban board: drag cards between columns, persist to localStorage"  →  5 high-level sprints
↓
IC Generator own context window

Builds against the contract — its own context, prompt and job. Proposes the contract, then writes code to satisfy it.

QA Evaluator own context window

Grades by using the app — Playwright clicks, screenshots, scores — not by reading diffs. Can throw it all out and restart.

contract.md — what Ralph never had

Before a line of code, generator & evaluator negotiate “done” into a file (scope, tests, edge cases — e.g. 27 criteria). The evaluator grades against that.

Generator  build →  Evaluator  ↻  ← critique · loop until it passes

“Tuning a standalone critic to be harsh is tractable; tuning a builder to be self-critical is not. Self-review is a trap.”

Ash Prabaker — exploit the gap between an LLM as critic vs. generator.
Source: Anthropic — “Build Agents That Run for Hours” (Prabaker & Wilson) · now official: a fresh-context reviewer beats self-review.
AITech LabThe build method
Two ways to work with agents

Two patterns to build with

Pattern 1 · Feature work

A pipeline of skills to build a feature well:

  • /brainstorming — shape the idea (obra · superpowers)
  • /grill-with-docs — pressure-test against the docs (Matt Pocock)
  • /make-me-understand — make sure you actually get it
Pattern 2 · Autonomous experiment

Research first, then a self-driving loop:

  • Define the 20/80 → deep research → a phased plan, one axis at a time, a hard “definition of done” per phase
  • Loop: define experiment → execute → monitor → conclude → relaunch
From the RLAIF hackathon deck — the phased plan.
AITech LabThe build method · close
Compress a routine into a skill

Wrap-up — one skill, four phases

The end-of-session routine, compressed into one /wrap-up skill that auto-applies and hands back a single report:

01 Ship

Commit, push, deploy — and sync the docs.

02 Memory

Capture what was learned; file it in the right tier.

03 Improve

Where did I redirect it? Fix the root, not the symptom.

04 Report

One consolidated summary of the session.

Same move for infra: compress change-validation into a skill, called inside a 3-skill loop.

AITech LabEvals
Evals

How it matures & where the signal lives

Capability vs behavior — measure both. Rigor climbs as the agent gets complex; in production the highest-value signal inverts.

How evals mature — rigor grows with complexity
Phase 1

Documented vibe-checks

~10 inputs; human thumbs + a written justification — the asset you scale later.

Phase 2

Measure to manage

LLM-judge (subjective) + deterministic code scorers (objective).

Phase 3

Whole-trace & tool calls

Score the full trace; target tool/MCP calls; mock externals, snapshot state.

Phase 4

Auto-discover

Topic-model production to surface failure modes — no longer hand-named.

Where the signal lives — value inverts
bottom

Benchmarks

capability — limited op. value.

middle

Scenario evals

realistic workflows, sandboxed.

top

Prod. telemetry

real users & systems — highest value.

★

North Star = reliability (latency, cost, recovery). Accuracy is an input, not the goal. Failure modes stack: coordination → tools → memory/safety.

“Evaluation is becoming the infrastructure — not testing, not QA.” Agent traces = the distributed tracing of autonomous work.

Sources: Phil Hetzel — Braintrust, maturity phases · Nishant Gupta — Meta MSL, production evals
AITech LabEvals · LLM as judge
Evals · LLM as judge

Never trust one vote

  • An LLM judging an output is noisy: ask the same judge twice, it changes its mind.
  • So sample it 3 or 5 times, an odd number, and take the majority vote.
  • A small law of large numbers, for the price of a few extra calls.
  • A small model like Haiku is usually enough: sharpen the question into a simple, unambiguous criterion first.
Always eval the judge

During observability, check the judge’s majority vote against your own labels. Only trust it past ≥ 80% agreement.[1] A judge is not trustworthy by default: “putting a robe and a cloak on an LLM doesn’t make it trustworthy”.[2] Judge outputs are discrete, so the ground-truth set is cheap to build.

AITech LabEvals · re-running production
Evals · re-running production

Evals = re-running production

A loop’s third phase is verify — and evals are that phase done seriously. Where’s the signal from? Not hand-written tests — from production itself, captured and replayed offline.

1
Capture

Record agent traces in production (or UAT) — real inputs, real users.

2
Diagnose

Find what went wrong — human annotation or automated tooling.

3
Replay offline

Pull those traces into the eval dataset, re-run them as evals.

4
Improve

Scores point the direction; ship the fix — then back to production.

“Don't think about evals as running tests. Think about evals like re-running production.”

Phil Hetzel — Braintrust. This is what lets the loop's Evaluation ingredient run unattended.
Source: Phil Hetzel — Braintrust, "The maturity phases of running evals"
AITech LabThe whole arc
What to take away

From a loop, to a harness, to loops

  • An agent is a loop: gather context → act → verify, until the goal is met. The model is a commodity — the harness is the engineering.
  • Stop hand-writing steps. Build loops that prompt themselves — and a loop is only as good as its verifier.
  • Two ways to work: skills-piped feature work, and autonomous experiment loops — both start from a sharp definition of done.

The bottleneck was never code. It’s knowing what “done” means.
